analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with expanded health savings accounts, private-insurance vouchers for Medicare, and interstate insurance sales.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died with zero cosponsors at the end of the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act in its entirety, then replace it with a set of market-oriented policies: much larger tax-deductible health savings accounts, an unlimited tax deduction for medical expenses, a tax credit for doctors who provide charity care, and vouchers so future Medicare beneficiaries would buy private insurance instead of traditional Medicare. It would also let insurers sell policies across state lines under the rules of whichever state they choose, and loosen the federal law requiring hospitals to screen and stabilize emergency patients. It never advanced past subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income households who can afford to fund health savings accounts and itemize deductions would gain the most in tax savings. Health insurers would gain a new federal revenue stream, since Medicare premium assistance would be paid into private plans, and the ability to sell policies built under the lightest-touch state's rules. Physicians gain a new tax credit for charity care.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would let anyone contribute to a health savings account, raise the deductible contribution limit to $10,000 ($20,000 for joint filers), and eliminate the penalty on non-medical withdrawals, making the accounts far more generous tax shelters.
It would remove the 7.5% income floor and other limits on the medical expense deduction and let Medicare-eligible people contribute to HSAs, expanding tax breaks for out-of-pocket health spending.

It would establish a Medicare Reform Premium Assistance Program that replaces Part A hospital entitlement with federal payments, computed at 120% of the median premium and deductible in the local individual market, usable only to buy private coverage or fund a medical savings account.

It would let insurers sell policies across state lines governed by the laws of a single 'primary state' they designate, exempting them from most other states' coverage mandates and rate rules, with a required disclosure that the policy may be cheaper because it lacks those benefits and protections.
It would give physicians a tax credit of up to $8,000 for providing at least 100 hours of pro bono care per year, and extend COBRA continuation coverage.

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions, who would lose the ACA's guaranteed-issue protections and could face policies that exclude their care or price it out. Medicare beneficiaries, whose guaranteed hospital coverage would be converted into a voucher that may not cover the same benefits. Hospital emergency departments, which would face weaker screening requirements. The Treasury, which would lose revenue from the expanded tax breaks.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and Medicare beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: Repealing the ACA's coverage-expansion title without an equivalent guarantee would remove protections that let people with pre-existing conditions buy insurance at standard rates, and the interstate-sales provision would let insurers sell policies exempt from other states' mandated benefits and consumer protections, the bill's own disclosure notice acknowledges such policies may skip those benefits.

Converting Medicare Part A into premium assistance based on the median individual-market premium could leave beneficiaries paying the difference between the voucher and the actual cost of comparable care, and enrollees in the program would be barred from Parts B and D.

The EMTALA changes would let hospitals satisfy the screening requirement with a triage-level check by a nurse or technician who decides no emergency exists, raising the risk that serious conditions are sent away without a full screening exam.
The HSA and medical-deduction expansions are largest for people with high incomes who have money to save and itemize, and the bill gives no cost estimate or offset for the lost revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains a few provisions that help individuals directly, like extending COBRA, paying doctors for charity care, and letting Medicare-age people fund HSAs. But its center of gravity is tax breaks that scale with income and a restructuring that shifts health-risk from insurers and government onto people with expensive conditions. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill provides no replacement guarantee for pre-existing conditions and no financing for its tax cuts.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight committees, then sent to subcommittees where it sat without a single hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Broun introduced the bill on March 20, 2012, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to eight committees the same day, including Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means.
Over the following six months it was referred to four subcommittees, with the last referral on September 26, 2012, and no further action was ever taken.
The bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with pre-existing conditions and Medicare beneficiaries kept the ACA protections and Medicare guarantees the bill would have repealed; insurers also retained the ACA-regulated market rather than the bill's lighter-touch regime. The bill was so lightly supported that its death changed little either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who kept ACA and Medicare protections

for.name: Rep. Paul Broun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House subcommittees of referral
against.role: Subcommittees on Health (Energy and Commerce), Health Employment Labor and Pensions (Education and Workforce), the Constitution and Courts (Judiciary), and Indian and Alaska Native Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and held no hearings or markups on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so support never took a measurable partisan shape.

industries.note: The bill would make private individual-market insurers the permanent channel for Medicare beneficiaries' coverage by converting Part A into premium assistance paid into private plans or medical savings accounts. It would also let insurers sell policies exempt from most state coverage mandates and consumer protections of secondary states, and its own required notice warns buyers such policies may cover less.

Expanding HSA contribution limits to $10,000-$20,000, removing the high-deductible-plan requirement, and eliminating the income floors on medical expense deductions create tax benefits that mostly accrue to people with high incomes and itemized deductions, while the cost of the lost revenue is not offset.

Doctors would earn a tax credit of up to $8,000 a year for pro bono care, encouraging uncompensated care that benefits patients. The credit is small relative to typical physician income, so the incentive is modest.

Looser EMTALA screening rules would let hospitals turn away some non-emergency patients and reduce uncompensated emergency care costs. Repealing the ACA's coverage expansion, however, would increase the number of uninsured patients hospitals treat without payment.
